toc.title: The Polyvagal Theory is not a modality
How emotions and thoughts keep you stuck
Yes, you can treat your body gently
Welcome it, and put it in your pocket

blocks.p: What do the shifts in your state actually look like from the inside, and how can you gently let yourself come out of a stuck state without sending yourself deeper into it? A listener's email is a great way into this. She wrote:

q: I've been listening to your podcast about a year. I was definitely skeptical at first, but am now very intrigued. I have investigated several other modalities as I've tried to heal some very significant childhood trauma for years without the benefit of professional therapy.

blocks.p: Thank you for giving it a shot. I think it's a good thing to have some skepticism, and to look up critiques of the Polyvagal Theory. There are a couple of serious ones out there.

blocks.h: The Polyvagal Theory is not a modality

blocks.p: I hear this from others, so let's be clear. The Polyvagal Theory is not a modality. It's not a therapeutic stance. It's not really a therapeutic or psychology theory. It's the science that lies underneath human connection: the science of mammalian connection and how we respond to danger. It's research, it's hypotheses with evidence to back them up, and it's ultimately potentially falsifiable. That's how science works.

So it's not a collection of techniques for a therapist to use. You can take that science and apply it to therapeutic modalities. It does illustrate a map of what change can look like as far as the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) is concerned, and it teaches us about the importance of co-regulation, which obviously plays into the therapy room. But we use it as a springboard. Dentists can apply it to their dentist room. Psychologists, doctors, nurses and teachers can apply it to what they do. It's the science that underlies human interaction, so for those of us in the service fields there's an obvious connection.
And there's a lot you can do in your own recovery without therapy. Learning the Polyvagal Theory is really foundational knowledge for that, and it's foundational for therapists too.
She went on:

q: My question is, is it possible in an extreme shutdown state to experience long-term loss of bodily sensations? I have heard other experts talk about numbing emotions as a result of extreme trauma, but I never heard anyone address the actual loss of physical sensations. For example, not feeling sensations of hunger or thirst, or not feeling temperature extremes like burns or frostbite to skin.

blocks.p: In general, I feel comfortable saying yes to this, maybe in particular with hunger. I've seen this in clients, and even with myself. You can probably relate: when you're in more of a shutdown state, you feel less hunger. The body is in a conservation state, so there's less need for resources to come in. There's probably going to be less of that sensation, that impulse to bring in new resources.

In shutdown, especially extreme shutdown, there's also less air coming in. Breathing becomes more shallow. Other physical sensations might change too. Someone might feel more cold, more internal coldness, because their blood pressure is significantly reduced in a shutdown state.

I don't know about temperature extremes, though. In the moment of an extreme shutdown, it would make sense, because part of shutdown is numbness, so maybe you are numb to something like frostbite. But that's the immediate survival function of shutdown. Long term, I don't know. Ultimately, I'm a therapist, and I have to stay in my lane. I can only go so far into the medical side of these things. Honestly, I don't really differentiate emotional and physical. I think they're pretty much one and the same, even though conceptually we separate them.
Her next question was about the order of things:

q: My understanding was our nervous system first feels sensation or impulse, then the emotion, and then responds. Is there a way to treat the body gently so that sensations come back into the window of tolerance and don't trigger one deeper in shutdown?

blocks.p: Here's how I understand the sequence of a neuroceptive state shift:

ol: Neuroception. There's a neuroceptive detection of safety or danger in the environment. This is unconscious, brain stem level stuff.
A shift on the ladder. If safety is detected, we go up the polyvagal ladder. If more danger is detected, we go down.
Sensations. Bodily sensations are felt with that shift.

An impulse. An impulse follows, or maybe happens at the same time. I've conceived of it as following the sensation, but it may be simultaneous, and I don't know how important that is. When we work backwards in therapy, someone will first feel a sensation, and then feel the impulse that's connected to the polyvagal state. If they can act on that impulse, that helps the state shift upward.
Emotion. When an impulse is frustrated, when it's unable to complete, we experience emotion. Emotions emerge when a bodily impulse is lingering and hasn't been able to complete.
Cognition. Along with the emotions come changes in cognition. Again, this might be simultaneous. I'd actually argue that it is.

blocks.p: Emotions are more consciously felt. We're aware of them, and we can name them more or less, not all the time, but there's more potential to. Emotions can also be minimized, ignored, stuffed down. We'll call those the more negative coping skills, or behavioral adaptations. According to Porges, behavioral adaptations are things we do to reduce our defensive state. We can also use them to numb out, or to reduce the intensity of our emotions, which are connected to a frustrated impulse, which is connected to a polyvagal state.

blocks.h: How emotions and thoughts keep you stuck

blocks.p: Emotions and cognitions both stem from the stuck state's impulses, and they both reinforce the stuck state as well.

Say you're stuck in a shutdown state, and you have an impulse to reduce stimulation, to be alone, maybe to hide until it's safe to come out. If you don't act on it, it just lives in the system and is probably felt as depression. The feelings are sadness, a lack of happiness, a lack of connection, loneliness.

Your cognitions shift too. You're going to have thoughts of how worthless you are. Not that I think you are, but you'll have thoughts describing a world or a self that's of low worth, or pointless, or very self-defeating. The memories that come to you, the thoughts you have about yourself: the flavor of your thoughts will be very numb and slow, probably.

These emotions and thoughts end up reinforcing the stuck state, and they may stop you from acting on the impulse within you. If your impulse is to isolate and be alone, and you listened to it, you might go to a comfortable spot where you feel some safety, where you can actually immobilize and mindfully attune to your shutdown state. You might give yourself quiet and feel it non-judgmentally.

But what tends to happen is that you feel the impulse, and rather than acting on it, you tell yourself, "Why am I so weak?" Or, "I wish I was stronger. I wish this would go away." Or, as you read this, you might say, "Justin, yeah, you're right, but there's no point. It's not going to get any better." Your thoughts stop you from mindfully acting on the impulse inside you.

blocks.h: Yes, you can treat your body gently

blocks.p: So is there a way to treat the body gently, so sensations come back into the window of tolerance and don't trigger you deeper into shutdown? Yes. But you have to build the strength of the vagal brake.

The vagal brake is the strength of your social engagement system: its ability to keep your heartbeat at a calmer pace, to tolerate climbing the polyvagal ladder, to tolerate the fear that may come with getting unstuck, especially out of a freeze, and to tolerate flight and fight energy coming back into your system. The stronger it is, the more capable you'll be of mindfully experiencing the stuck state's impulses and sensations.
You can work your way in from the outside:

ol: Notice the flavor of your thoughts. You might be able to say, "My thoughts are very empty," or "hopeless." Hopeless is a good word for it. Or, in a fight state, "I can recognize my thoughts are full of blame and judgment, maybe shaming of others, not taking responsibility for my choices."
Recognize your emotions. Mindfully recognize the emotions you have inside you.
Feel the sensations underneath. Go a bit deeper and feel the sensations that underlie your emotions.
Feel and act on the impulse. Maybe go a bit deeper still, and actually feel and act on the impulse, or impulses, inside you.

blocks.p: To gently tolerate those sensations, you have to be able to stay grounded in your safety state. You have to be able to do this mindfulness work from a place of curiosity: not judgment, not evaluation, not trying to stop it, but actual curiosity, so you can welcome it.

You may also need to accept co-regulation from somebody else, someone in your life who can provide safety cues from them to you, like in therapy especially. And you may need to know your safety anchors: what helps you feel grounded and in the present moment, what helps you feel anchored, what helps you feel safe, and what that feels like.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: It's possible to have a greater window of tolerance, to feel these stuck defensive sensations. But you have to build the capacity to do so, and it's not easy. It's a gradual process of building your capacity to be mindful of what's happening within you, knowing when to start this kind of mindfulness work, knowing when to stop, knowing what your line is, knowing what brings you to safety, and then putting those pieces together and setting yourself up for success.

One participant in one of my courses found the movement part too much for her. She had a lot of reluctance about it. But she wanted to go through things in order, and she found a way to make it work for her in a tolerable way. She was able to identify when to start, when to stop, how to stay grounded in safety, and how to get through the steps. There was enough mindfulness of her capacity, of her tolerance, to make it work.
Basically, you have to identify what safety feels like for you. Not me, you. Practice it, be in it, practice it. That will help you build your capacity to handle more difficult things.
That's my priority as a therapist. Are you grounded in safety? If yes, can you make the choice to delve further? Because it is a choice you make.

There is a way to handle these things more gently. You don't have to plow through them. I don't think it's helpful to just plow through the stuck defensive stuff, and it could actually be re-traumatizing if you're not ready for it.

If what you're doing sends you into your shutdown state all over again, if you come out and then go back down, that's probably a good indication that it's too much for your system right now. That could even be talking to your therapist about the event that led to a stuck traumatic state, or sharing the trauma narrative. That could easily send someone back into shutdown.

I've heard this from people who've done EMDR, and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy as well. They tell me they just numbed out and shut down, because they were expected to tell the story and it was too much. They'll say, "I don't know how I got through it. I just kind of got through it, but I don't think it really helped me." So I'd encourage my peers, my fellow therapists, to be mindful of that.

You could also send yourself into shutdown if you try to look inward, do that work of journeying inward, maybe meditating on your emotions or sensations, or looking at past events, before you're ready to. I don't recommend that. Going back into shutdown that way is just reinforcing the trauma.

I've even heard from people that doing yoga or some type of movement before they were ready, or in the wrong context, or without things being normalized, sent them into a shutdown state. So to my yoga peers, and I know you all do this already: normalizing ahead of time, and giving people permission not to participate in certain parts, might give them the capacity to make a clear choice. Knowing you can choose not to is a gentle way of approaching these things.

blocks.h: Welcome it, and put it in your pocket

blocks.p: It's completely okay to welcome a shutdown. That might sound weird, but I think that's what being gentle with this comes down to. These feelings are already there, so you might as well welcome them to be there with you.
If you're filled with anger, it's already there. You can do the best you can to keep your mind off it, and that's fine. But at some point, it's okay to gently tell yourself:

"Look, I feel this way. I feel this way for a reason. It's okay to feel this way, and I'm just going to let it be there for a little bit. I'm not going to reject it. I'm not going to do anything about it. I'm not going to try to fix it. I'm not going to examine it. I'm just going to let it be there, and notice it, while I also do something that's more grounding, or focus on something else."
So it's not about rejecting. It's about eventually, gently saying to your emotion or those sensations, "Hey, you're welcome to hang out with me." Something like:

"I feel you, sadness and aloneness and grief, maybe longing, missing. I feel you. I recognize you're there. Fighting it isn't doing any good, so you can hang out with me. I'm going to put you in my pocket. You can follow me around all day. I know you're there anyway. I'm not going to reject you. I know you're there for a reason, so you're welcome to hang out with me. But I've got stuff to do. And it's also okay for me to feel safe. It's also okay for me to feel some connection, or relaxation, or joy, or happiness, or playfulness."
It's okay to have both of these things, and to invite both of them, or more, gently, to be there with you. Maybe that's what being gentle with your sensations and your emotions sounds like.
